claim: Straight-tusked elephants Palaeoloxodon spp. were widespread across Eurasia during the Pleistocene.
source: The straight-tusked elephants Palaeoloxodon spp. were widespread across Eurasia during the Pleistocene.
evidence: This is a statement about the geographic and temporal distribution of Palaeoloxodon, drawing from established paleontological knowledge.

claim: Phylogenetic reconstructions using morphological traits have grouped Palaeoloxodon with Asian elephants (Elephas maximus).
source: Phylogenetic reconstructions using morphological traits have grouped them with Asian elephants (Elephas maximus), and many paleontologists place Palaeoloxodon within Elephas.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior scientific work on morphological phylogenetics.

claim: Many paleontologists place Palaeoloxodon within Elephas.
source: Phylogenetic reconstructions using morphological traits have grouped them with Asian elephants (Elephas maximus), and many paleontologists place Palaeoloxodon within Elephas.
evidence: This claim reflects the consensus view in paleontology prior to this study.

claim: Full mitochondrial genomes were recovered from four P. antiquus fossils.
source: Here, we report the recovery of full mitochondrial genomes from four and partial nuclear genomes from two P. antiquus fossils.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study.

claim: Partial nuclear genomes were recovered from two P. antiquus fossils.
source: Here, we report the recovery of full mitochondrial genomes from four and partial nuclear genomes from two P. antiquus fossils.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study.

claim: The P. antiquus fossils were collected at two sites in Germany: Neumark-Nord and Weimar-Ehringsdorf.
source: These fossils were collected at two sites in Germany, Neumark-Nord and Weimar-Ehringsdorf, and likely date to interglacial periods ~120 and ~244 thousand years ago, respectively.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the provenance of the samples.

claim: The Neumark-Nord fossils likely date to an interglacial period approximately 120 thousand years ago.
source: These fossils were collected at two sites in Germany, Neumark-Nord and Weimar-Ehringsdorf, and likely date to interglacial periods ~120 and ~244 thousand years ago, respectively.
evidence: This claim is based on dating analyses performed in the study.

claim: The Weimar-Ehringsdorf fossils likely date to an interglacial period approximately 244 thousand years ago.
source: These fossils were collected at two sites in Germany, Neumark-Nord and Weimar-Ehringsdorf, and likely date to interglacial periods ~120 and ~244 thousand years ago, respectively.
evidence: This claim is based on dating analyses performed in the study.

claim: Nuclear and mitochondrial DNA analyses suggest that P. antiquus was a close relative of extant African forest elephants (Loxodonta cyclotis).
source: Unexpectedly, nuclear and mitochondrial DNA analyses suggest that P. antiquus was a close relative of extant African forest elephants (Loxodonta cyclotis).
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by phylogenetic analyses of DNA sequences.

claim: Species previously referred to Palaeoloxodon are most parsimoniously explained as having diverged from the lineage of Loxodonta.
source: Species previously referred to Palaeoloxodon are thus most parsimoniously explained as having diverged from the lineage of Loxodonta, indicating that Loxodonta has not been constrained to Africa.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the phylogenetic results.

claim: Loxodonta has not been constrained to Africa.
source: Species previously referred to Palaeoloxodon are thus most parsimoniously explained as having diverged from the lineage of Loxodonta, indicating that Loxodonta has not been constrained to Africa.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that Palaeoloxodon, found in Eurasia, belongs to the Loxodonta lineage.

claim: The current picture of elephant evolution is in need of substantial revision.
source: Our results demonstrate that the current picture of elephant evolution is in need of substantial revision.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the unexpected phylogenetic placement of Palaeoloxodon.

claim: The last major radiation within Proboscidea in the late Miocene in Africa gave rise to the family Elephantidae.
source: In the late Miocene in Africa, the last of several major radiations within Proboscidea gave rise to the family Elephantidae, which comprises living elephants and their extinct relatives including mammoths (genus Mammuthus) and various dwarf elephant species from Mediterranean islands.
evidence: This is a statement based on established paleontological knowledge.

claim: The family Elephantidae comprises living elephants and their extinct relatives including mammoths and various dwarf elephant species from Mediterranean islands.
source: In the late Miocene in Africa, the last of several major radiations within Proboscidea gave rise to the family Elephantidae, which comprises living elephants and their extinct relatives including mammoths (genus Mammuthus) and various dwarf elephant species from Mediterranean islands.
evidence: This is a statement based on established paleontological knowledge.

claim: The three living elephant species are the African savanna elephant (Loxodonta africana), the African forest elephant (L. cyclotis), and the Asian elephant (Elephas maximus).
source: The three living elephant species (the African savanna elephant, Loxodonta africana, the African forest elephant, L. cyclotis and the Asian elephant, Elephas maximus), represent the last remnants of this family and of the formerly much more widely distributed and species-rich order Proboscidea.
evidence: This is a statement of established taxonomic knowledge.

claim: The three living elephant species represent the last remnants of the family Elephantidae and the order Proboscidea.
source: The three living elephant species (the African savanna elephant, Loxodonta africana, the African forest elephant, L. cyclotis and the Asian elephant, Elephas maximus), represent the last remnants of this family and of the formerly much more widely distributed and species-rich order Proboscidea.
evidence: This is a statement based on established paleontological and taxonomic knowledge.

claim: Palaeoloxodon appears in Eurasia around 0.75 million years ago.
source: Apart from mammoths, the elephant genus with the most abundant fossil record in Eurasia is Palaeoloxodon (straight-tusked elephants; Figure 1), which appears in Eurasia around 0.75 million years ago (Ma) (Lister, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lister, 2016.

claim: Based on morphological analyses, Palaeoloxodon is widely accepted as being more closely related to the extant Asian elephant than to mammoths or extant African elephants.
source: Based on morphological analyses, Palaeoloxodon is widely accepted as being more closely related to the extant Asian elephant than to mammoths or extant African elephants (Shoshani et al., 2007; Todd, 2010) and is often subsumed into the genus Elephas (Maglio, 1973; Sanders et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to morphological studies.

claim: Palaeoloxodon is often subsumed into the genus Elephas.
source: Based on morphological analyses, Palaeoloxodon is widely accepted as being more closely related to the extant Asian elephant than to mammoths or extant African elephants (Shoshani et al., 2007; Todd, 2010) and is often subsumed into the genus Elephas (Maglio, 1973; Sanders et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to taxonomic literature.

claim: Palaeoloxodon probably comprised several species across its range from Western Europe to Japan.
source: Across its range from Western Europe to Japan, Palaeoloxodon probably comprised several species (Shoshani et al., 2007), and, based on morphological comparisons, all of them are considered to be derived from the African Palaeoloxodon (or Elephas) recki (Maglio, 1973; Saegusa and Gilbert, 2008), which was the predominant proboscidean lineage in Africa during the Pliocene and Pleistocene but went extinct around 100 thousand years ago (ka) (Owen-Smith, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shoshani et al., 2007.

claim: Based on morphological comparisons, all Palaeoloxodon species are considered to be derived from the African Palaeoloxodon (or Elephas) recki.
source: Across its range from Western Europe to Japan, Palaeoloxodon probably comprised several species (Shoshani et al., 2007), and, based on morphological comparisons, all of them are considered to be derived from the African Palaeoloxodon (or Elephas) recki (Maglio, 1973; Saegusa and Gilbert, 2008), which was the predominant proboscidean lineage in Africa during the Pliocene and Pleistocene but went extinct around 100 thousand years ago (ka) (Owen-Smith, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to morphological studies.

claim: Palaeoloxodon (or Elephas) recki was the predominant proboscidean lineage in Africa during the Pliocene and Pleistocene.
source: Across its range from Western Europe to Japan, Palaeoloxodon probably comprised several species (Shoshani et al., 2007), and, based on morphological comparisons, all of them are considered to be derived from the African Palaeoloxodon (or Elephas) recki (Maglio, 1973; Saegusa and Gilbert, 2008), which was the predominant proboscidean lineage in Africa during the Pliocene and Pleistocene but went extinct around 100 thousand years ago (ka) (Owen-Smith, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement based on the fossil record, supported by a citation.

claim: Palaeoloxodon (or Elephas) recki went extinct around 100 thousand years ago.
source: Across its range from Western Europe to Japan, Palaeoloxodon probably comprised several species (Shoshani et al., 2007), and, based on morphological comparisons, all of them are considered to be derived from the African Palaeoloxodon (or Elephas) recki (Maglio, 1973; Saegusa and Gilbert, 2008), which was the predominant proboscidean lineage in Africa during the Pliocene and Pleistocene but went extinct around 100 thousand years ago (ka) (Owen-Smith, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Owen-Smith, 2013.

claim: Straight-tusked elephants may have survived in mainland Eurasia until around 35 ka.
source: Straight-tusked elephants may have survived in mainland Eurasia until around 35 ka, although the youngest reliably dated remains are from the last interglacial, 115–130 ka (Stuart, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stuart, 2005.

claim: The youngest reliably dated remains of straight-tusked elephants are from the last interglacial, 115–130 ka.
source: Straight-tusked elephants may have survived in mainland Eurasia until around 35 ka, although the youngest reliably dated remains are from the last interglacial, 115–130 ka (Stuart, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stuart, 2005.

claim: Recent technological progress has pushed back the temporal limit of ancient DNA research.
source: Recent technological progress has pushed back the temporal limit of ancient DNA research, enabling, for example, recovery of a low coverage genome of a ~700,000 year-old horse preserved in permafrost (Orlando et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the field of ancient DNA research, supported by a citation.

claim: A low coverage genome of a ~700,000 year-old horse preserved in permafrost has been recovered.
source: Recent technological progress has pushed back the temporal limit of ancient DNA research, enabling, for example, recovery of a low coverage genome of a ~700,000 year-old horse preserved in permafrost (Orlando et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Orlando et al., 2013.

claim: For more temperate regions, evidence of DNA preservation reaching far beyond the last glacial period is limited to a single locality, Sima de los Huesos in Spain.
source: For more temperate regions, however, evidence of DNA preservation reaching far beyond the last glacial period is still limited to a single locality, Sima de los Huesos in Spain, where DNA has been recovered from ~430 ka old hominin and bear remains (Dabney et al., 2013; Meyer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on Sima de los Huesos.

claim: DNA has been recovered from ~430 ka old hominin and bear remains at Sima de los Huesos in Spain.
source: For more temperate regions, however, evidence of DNA preservation reaching far beyond the last glacial period is still limited to a single locality, Sima de los Huesos in Spain, where DNA has been recovered from ~430 ka old hominin and bear remains (Dabney et al., 2013; Meyer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dabney et al., 2013 and Meyer et al., 2016.

claim: Recent advances in ancient DNA extraction have improved access to highly degraded DNA.
source: While genetic analyses of the extinct interglacial fauna remain a challenging undertaking, recent advances in ancient DNA extraction (Dabney et al., 2013) and sequencing library construction (Meyer et al., 2012) have improved access to highly degraded DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to methodological papers.

claim: Recent advances in sequencing library construction have improved access to highly degraded DNA.
source: While genetic analyses of the extinct interglacial fauna remain a challenging undertaking, recent advances in ancient DNA extraction (Dabney et al., 2013) and sequencing library construction (Meyer et al., 2012) have improved access to highly degraded DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to methodological papers.

claim: Three P. antiquus fossils from Neumark-Nord were unambiguously assigned to P. antiquus based on their morphology.
source: Three of these, which were all unambiguously assigned to P. antiquus based on their morphology, were from Neumark-Nord (NN) 1 in Germany, a fossil-rich site that has been proposed to date to MIS 5e (~120 ka) or MIS 7 (~244 ka) or both (Mania, 2010; Schüler, 2010; Penkman, 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about the morphological identification of the specimens.

claim: Neumark-Nord 1 has been proposed to date to MIS 5e (~120 ka) or MIS 7 (~244 ka) or both.
source: Three of these, which were all unambiguously assigned to P. antiquus based on their morphology, were from Neumark-Nord (NN) 1 in Germany, a fossil-rich site that has been proposed to date to MIS 5e (~120 ka) or MIS 7 (~244 ka) or both (Mania, 2010; Schüler, 2010; Penkman, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to dating studies.

claim: Neumark-Nord 1 has yielded one of the largest collections of P. antiquus remains known to date.
source: This site has yielded one of the largest collections of P. antiquus remains known to date.
evidence: This is a statement about the fossil record at the site.

claim: The fourth fossil was recovered during recent active mining in the travertine deposits of Weimar-Ehringsdorf, Germany.
source: The fourth fossil was recovered during recent active mining in the travertine deposits of Weimar-Ehringsdorf (WE), Germany, a quarry that has for more than a century yielded a rich collection of fossils representing a typical European interglacial fauna (Kahlke, 1975).
evidence: This is a statement about the provenance of the specimen.

claim: Weimar-Ehringsdorf has for more than a century yielded a rich collection of fossils representing a typical European interglacial fauna.
source: The fourth fossil was recovered during recent active mining in the travertine deposits of Weimar-Ehringsdorf (WE), Germany, a quarry that has for more than a century yielded a rich collection of fossils representing a typical European interglacial fauna (Kahlke, 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kahlke, 1975.

claim: Weimar-Ehringsdorf is best known for the discovery of Neanderthal remains in the early 20th century.
source: Weimar-Ehringsdorf is best known for the discovery of Neanderthal remains in the early 20th century, and the assemblage is dated to MIS 7 (Mallick and Frank, 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about the historical significance of the site.

claim: The Weimar-Ehringsdorf assemblage is dated to MIS 7.
source: Weimar-Ehringsdorf is best known for the discovery of Neanderthal remains in the early 20th century, and the assemblage is dated to MIS 7 (Mallick and Frank, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mallick and Frank, 2002.

claim: The Palaeoloxodon bone fragment from Weimar-Ehringsdorf is morphologically undiagnostic with respect to species.
source: The Paleoloxodon bone fragment from Weimar-Ehringsdorf is morphologically undiagnostic with respect to species.
evidence: This is a statement about the morphological characteristics of the specimen.

claim: The Weimar-Ehringsdorf bone fragment was found in the Lower Travertine, which was dated to ~233 ka.
source: However, it was found in the Lower Travertine, which was dated to ~233 ka (Schüler, 2003) and where P. antiquus is the only elephantid found so far.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schüler, 2003.

claim: P. antiquus is the only elephantid found so far in the Lower Travertine at Weimar-Ehringsdorf.
source: However, it was found in the Lower Travertine, which was dated to ~233 ka (Schüler, 2003) and where P. antiquus is the only elephantid found so far.
evidence: This is a statement about the fossil record at the site.

claim: All four P. antiquus specimens show short fragment lengths.
source: All sequences show short fragment lengths (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and signals of cytosine deamination compatible with the old age of the specimens (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: All four P. antiquus specimens show signals of cytosine deamination compatible with the old age of the specimens.
source: All sequences show short fragment lengths (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and signals of cytosine deamination compatible with the old age of the specimens (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: A phylogeny was inferred using the four Palaeoloxodon mitochondrial genomes and mitochondrial genomes from 16 M. primigenius, 2 E. maximus and 13 Loxodonta individuals.
source: We inferred a phylogeny using the four Paleoloxodon mitochondrial genomes and mitochondrial genomes from 16 M. primigenius, 2 E. maximus and 13 Loxodonta individuals.
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic analysis performed.

claim: The Loxodonta individuals used in the phylogeny were chosen for a diversity of haplotypes, including forest elephant derived ('F-clade') haplotypes as well as 'S-clade' haplotypes found only among savanna elephants.
source: The latter were chosen for a diversity of haplotypes, including forest elephant derived ('F-clade') haplotypes as well as 'S-clade' haplotypes found only among savanna elephants (Debruyne, 2005).
evidence: This is a description of the sampling strategy, with a citation to Debruyne, 2005.

claim: An estimated divergence of the African elephant lineage from that of Asian elephants and mammoths of 6.6–8.6 Ma was used for calibration.
source: For calibration, we used an estimated divergence of the African elephant lineage from that of Asian elephants and mammoths of 6.6–8.6 Ma (Rohland et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a description of the calibration used in the phylogenetic analysis, supported by a citation.

claim: P. antiquus did not cluster with E. maximus, as hypothesized from morphological analyses.
source: Surprisingly, P. antiquus did not cluster with E. maximus, as hypothesized from morphological analyses.
evidence: This is a statement of the phylogenetic result, contrasting with prior expectations.

claim: P. antiquus fell within the mito-genetic diversity of extant L. cyclotis, with very high statistical support.
source: Instead, it fell within the mito-genetic diversity of extant L. cyclotis, with very high statistical support (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statement of the phylogenetic result, supported by Figure 2.

claim: The four straight-tusked elephants did not cluster together within the mitochondrial clade, but formed two separate lineages.
source: The four straight-tusked elephants did not cluster together within this mitochondrial clade, but formed two separate lineages that share a common ancestor with an extant L. cyclotis lineage 0.7–1.6 Ma (NN) and 1.5–3.0 Ma (WE) ago, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement of the phylogenetic result.

claim: The Neumark-Nord P. antiquus specimens share a common ancestor with an extant L. cyclotis lineage 0.7–1.6 Ma ago.
source: The four straight-tusked elephants did not cluster together within this mitochondrial clade, but formed two separate lineages that share a common ancestor with an extant L. cyclotis lineage 0.7–1.6 Ma (NN) and 1.5–3.0 Ma (WE) ago, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement of the phylogenetic result.

claim: The Weimar-Ehringsdorf P. antiquus specimen shares a common ancestor with an extant L. cyclotis lineage 1.5–3.0 Ma ago.
source: The four straight-tusked elephants did not cluster together within this mitochondrial clade, but formed two separate lineages that share a common ancestor with an extant L. cyclotis lineage 0.7–1.6 Ma (NN) and 1.5–3.0 Ma (WE) ago, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement of the phylogenetic result.

claim: Mitochondrial DNA represents a single, maternally inherited locus and does not reflect the full evolutionary history of populations or species.
source: However, mitochondrial DNA represents a single, maternally inherited locus and does not reflect the full evolutionary history of populations or species.
evidence: This is a statement of established genetic knowledge.

claim: The transfer of mitochondrial DNA between hybridizing species is not unusual when gene flow is strongly male-mediated.
source: Furthermore, the transfer of mitochondrial DNA between hybridizing species is not unusual when gene flow is strongly male-mediated (Petit and Excoffier, 2009; Li et al., 2016; Cahill et al., 2013), as is the case with elephants.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on gene flow and mitochondrial introgression.

claim: Gene flow in elephants is strongly male-mediated.
source: Furthermore, the transfer of mitochondrial DNA between hybridizing species is not unusual when gene flow is strongly male-mediated (Petit and Excoffier, 2009; Li et al., 2016; Cahill et al., 2013), as is the case with elephants.
evidence: This is a statement about elephant biology, supported by the context of the citations.

claim: Mitochondrial sequences of the F-clade have been found in some L. africana individuals.
source: For example, mitochondrial sequences of the F-clade have also been found in some L. africana individuals (Debruyne, 2005) despite the very substantial divergence of their nuclear genomes (Roca et al., 2005; Rohland et al., 2010), a pattern that has been attributed to mitochondrial gene flow from forest to savanna elephants (Roca et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Debruyne, 2005.

claim: L. africana and L. cyclotis show very substantial divergence of their nuclear genomes.
source: For example, mitochondrial sequences of the F-clade have also been found in some L. africana individuals (Debruyne, 2005) despite the very substantial divergence of their nuclear genomes (Roca et al., 2005; Rohland et al., 2010), a pattern that has been attributed to mitochondrial gene flow from forest to savanna elephants (Roca et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Roca et al., 2005 and Rohland et al., 2010.

claim: The presence of F-clade mitochondrial sequences in some L. africana individuals has been attributed to mitochondrial gene flow from forest to savanna elephants.
source: For example, mitochondrial sequences of the F-clade have also been found in some L. africana individuals (Debruyne, 2005) despite the very substantial divergence of their nuclear genomes (Roca et al., 2005; Rohland et al., 2010), a pattern that has been attributed to mitochondrial gene flow from forest to savanna elephants (Roca et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Roca et al., 2005.

claim: Shotgun sequencing of DNA libraries was performed from the two best-preserved Neumark-Nord individuals (a petrous bone and a molar) to recover nuclear DNA sequences.
source: We therefore performed shotgun sequencing of DNA libraries prepared from the two best-preserved NN individuals (a petrous bone and a molar) to recover nuclear DNA sequences.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: 39% of the sequence reads generated from the petrous bone specimen were identified as elephant when mapped to the L. africana reference genome.
source: When mapped to the L. africana reference genome, 39% and 28% of the sequence reads generated from these specimens were identified as elephant, respectively (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statement of the sequencing results.

claim: 28% of the sequence reads generated from the molar specimen were identified as elephant when mapped to the L. africana reference genome.
source: When mapped to the L. africana reference genome, 39% and 28% of the sequence reads generated from these specimens were identified as elephant, respectively (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statement of the sequencing results.

claim: A neighbor-joining phylogenetic tree based on ~770M (petrous) and ~210M (molar) base pairs of P. antiquus nuclear DNA placed P. antiquus and L. cyclotis as sister taxa to the exclusion of L. africana.
source: A neighbor-joining phylogenetic tree based on ~770M (petrous) and ~210M (molar) base pairs of P. antiquus nuclear DNA placed P. antiquus and L. cyclotis as sister taxa to the exclusion of L. africana (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statement of the phylogenetic result, supported by Figure 2.

claim: A tree with identical topology to the neighbor-joining tree was obtained using coding sequences only and a maximum likelihood approach.
source: A tree with identical topology was obtained using coding sequences only and a maximum likelihood approach (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a statement of the phylogenetic result, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: All nodes in the nuclear trees show maximal bootstrap support.
source: Despite the high sequence error rates associated with the low-coverage genomes generated from the P. antiquus specimens, all nodes in the nuclear trees show maximal bootstrap support.
evidence: This is a statement of the statistical support for the phylogenetic results.

claim: The mitochondrial and nuclear phylogenies support a sister group relationship between P. antiquus and L. cyclotis.
source: The mitochondrial and nuclear phylogenies thus support a sister group relationship between P. antiquus and L. cyclotis.
evidence: This is a summary of the phylogenetic results.

claim: The three Neumark-Nord specimens show highly similar mitogenome sequences.
source: Given that the three NN specimens show highly similar mitogenome sequences, we considered whether the sites date to different interglacials.
evidence: This is a statement of the sequence similarity observed.

claim: Electron Spin Resonance (ESR) dating of tooth enamel suggests an age of ~117 ka (range 97–142 ka) for the NN1 layers from which the samples originate.
source: Electron Spin Resonance (ESR) dating of tooth enamel has been applied to both sites, suggesting an age of ~117 ka (range 97–142 ka [Schüler, 2010]) for the NN1 layers from which our samples originate and of 233 ka (range 216–250 ka [Schüler, 2003]) for the WE specimen.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schüler, 2010.

claim: Electron Spin Resonance (ESR) dating of tooth enamel suggests an age of 233 ka (range 216–250 ka) for the Weimar-Ehringsdorf specimen.
source: Electron Spin Resonance (ESR) dating of tooth enamel has been applied to both sites, suggesting an age of ~117 ka (range 97–142 ka [Schüler, 2010]) for the NN1 layers from which our samples originate and of 233 ka (range 216–250 ka [Schüler, 2003]) for the WE specimen.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schüler, 2003.

claim: Amino acid racemization of snail opercula was used to better estimate the age of the NN1 site.
source: In order to better estimate the age of the NN1 site, we used amino acid racemization of snail opercula (Penkman et al., 2011), including samples from the continental Eemian type-site of Amersfoort (Zagwijn, 1961) (Figure 2—source data 1), which is correlated with MIS 5e (Cleveringa et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a description of the dating method used, supported by citations.

claim: The NN1 opercula show similar (perhaps slightly lower) levels of biomolecular degradation compared to Amersfoort, suggesting an Eemian age for NN1.
source: The NN1 opercula show similar (perhaps slightly lower) levels of biomolecular degradation compared to Amersfoort, suggesting an Eemian age for NN1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a statement of the dating result, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: NN1 shows very similar levels of amino acid racemization in intra-crystalline protein decomposition as NN2, indicating that both sites are of the same age.
source: Importantly, NN1 shows very similar levels of amino acid racemization in intra-crystalline protein decomposition as a second site at Neumark-Nord (NN2), indicating that both sites are of the same age.
evidence: This is a statement of the dating result.

claim: Considerable evidence supports an Eemian age for NN2, including palaeomagnetic data that shows a correlation with the MIS 5e Blake event and thermoluminescence dating of flint to ~126 ± 6 ka.
source: Considerable evidence supports an Eemian age for NN2, including palaeomagnetic data that shows a correlation with the MIS 5e Blake event and thermoluminescence dating of flint to ~126 ± 6 ka (Sier et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sier et al., 2011.

claim: The amino acid racemization results indicate an Eemian age also for NN1.
source: These results therefore indicate an Eemian age also for NN1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the amino acid racemization data.

claim: The Weimar-Ehringsdorf specimen likely dates to the previous interglacial (before the Eemian).
source: Since the WE specimen likely dates to the previous interglacial, this suggests that the very different mitogenomes between WE and NN1 may reflect the contraction and re-expansion of the range of P. antiquus across glacial cycles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dating results.

claim: The very different mitogenomes between Weimar-Ehringsdorf and NN1 may reflect the contraction and re-expansion of the range of P. antiquus across glacial cycles.
source: Since the WE specimen likely dates to the previous interglacial, this suggests that the very different mitogenomes between WE and NN1 may reflect the contraction and re-expansion of the range of P. antiquus across glacial cycles.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the phylogenetic and dating results.

claim: The strongly supported mitochondrial and nuclear DNA phylogenies clearly demonstrate that Palaeoloxodon antiquus is more closely related to Loxodonta than to Elephas.
source: Our results have implications both for understanding elephant evolutionary history and for the use of morphological data to decipher phylogenetic relationships among elephants. The strongly supported mitochondrial and nuclear DNA phylogenies clearly demonstrate that Palaeoloxodon antiquus is more closely related to Loxodonta than to Elephas (Figure 3), suggesting that Elephas antiquus should not be used synonymously for Paleoloxodon antiquus when referring to the taxon.
evidence: This is a summary of the phylogenetic results, supported by Figure 3.

claim: Elephas antiquus should not be used synonymously for Palaeoloxodon antiquus when referring to the taxon.
source: The strongly supported mitochondrial and nuclear DNA phylogenies clearly demonstrate that Palaeoloxodon antiquus is more closely related to Loxodonta than to Elephas (Figure 3), suggesting that Elephas antiquus should not be used synonymously for Paleoloxodon antiquus when referring to the taxon.
evidence: This is a taxonomic recommendation based on the phylogenetic results.

claim: The new phylogeny suggests a remarkable degree of evolutionary transformation, from an ancestor that possessed the features of the cranium and dentition of Loxodonta to a descendant that is highly similar to Elephas in many morphological features.
source: The new phylogeny suggests a remarkable degree of evolutionary transformation, from an ancestor that possessed the features of the cranium and dentition of Loxodonta, shared by both L. africana and L. cyclotis (Maglio, 1973; Sanders et al., 2010), to a descendant that is highly similar to Elephas (sensu stricto, the lineage of the Asian elephant) in many morphological features.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the phylogenetic results in light of morphological data, supported by citations.

claim: Currently available genomic data from elephantids only allow for reconstructing the broad picture of elephant evolution.
source: However, it should be noted that currently available genomic data from elephantids only allow for reconstructing the broad picture of elephant evolution.
evidence: This is a caveat about the limitations of the current data.

claim: More complex evolutionary scenarios are conceivable, which might explain the presence of some Elephas-like traits in P. antiquus.
source: More complex evolutionary scenarios are conceivable, which might explain the presence of some Elephas-like traits in P. antiquus.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about alternative explanations.

claim: Complex evolutionary scenarios could involve gene flow, as has been shown for L. africana and L. cyclotis based on mitochondrial evidence.
source: These could for example involve gene flow, as has been shown for L. africana and L. cyclotis based on mitochondrial evidence (Roca et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to a study on gene flow.

claim: The very large effective population size of the forest elephants could have allowed the retention of ancestral traits by incomplete lineage sorting.
source: In addition, the very large effective population size of the forest elephants (Rohland et al., 2010) could have allowed the retention of ancestral traits by incomplete lineage sorting.
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to a study on population genetics.

claim: The molecular results presented urge for a re-examination of morphology across the Elephantidae.
source: In summary, the molecular results presented here urge for a re-examination of morphology across the Elephantidae.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the phylogenetic results.

claim: Re-examination of morphology is especially important as the fossil record for elephants dates back several million years, well beyond the survival of ancient DNA.
source: This is especially important as the fossil record for elephants dates back several million years, well beyond the survival of ancient DNA.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of ancient DNA and the importance of morphology.

claim: If P. recki is indeed ancestral to P. antiquus and thus also represents a member of the Loxodonta lineage, the interpretation of the fossil record of elephantids in Africa is in strong need of revision.
source: If, for example, P. recki, which was the most abundant Pleistocene elephant species in Africa, is indeed ancestral to P. antiquus and thus also represents a member of the Loxodonta lineage, the interpretation of the fossil record of elephantids in Africa is in strong need of revision.
evidence: This is a conditional statement about the implications of the phylogenetic results.

claim: P. recki was the most abundant Pleistocene elephant species in Africa.
source: If, for example, P. recki, which was the most abundant Pleistocene elephant species in Africa, is indeed ancestral to P. antiquus and thus also represents a member of the Loxodonta lineage, the interpretation of the fossil record of elephantids in Africa is in strong need of revision.
evidence: This is a statement about the fossil record.

claim: The genera Mammuthus and Elephas had their origin in Africa.
source: Furthermore, in contrast to the genera Mammuthus and Elephas, which also had their origin in Africa, the lineage of Loxodonta is generally assumed never to have left Africa.
evidence: This is a statement based on established paleontological knowledge.

claim: The lineage of Loxodonta is generally assumed never to have left Africa.
source: Furthermore, in contrast to the genera Mammuthus and Elephas, which also had their origin in Africa, the lineage of Loxodonta is generally assumed never to have left Africa.
evidence: This is a statement of the prior consensus view.

claim: Osborn, 1942 placed Palaeoloxodon in the Loxodontinae on the basis of several cranial characters.
source: Although Osborn, 1942 placed Palaeoloxodon in the Loxodontinae on the basis of several cranial characters, later authors (Shoshani et al., 2007; Todd, 2010) have rejected this placement in favor of a placement in Elephantinae, restricting Loxodonta (and Loxodontinae) geographically to Africa.
evidence: This is a statement about the history of taxonomic classification, supported by a citation.

claim: Later authors have rejected Osborn's placement of Palaeoloxodon in Loxodontinae in favor of a placement in Elephantinae, restricting Loxodonta (and Loxodontinae) geographically to Africa.
source: Although Osborn, 1942 placed Palaeoloxodon in the Loxodontinae on the basis of several cranial characters, later authors (Shoshani et al., 2007; Todd, 2010) have rejected this placement in favor of a placement in Elephantinae, restricting Loxodonta (and Loxodontinae) geographically to Africa.
evidence: This is a statement about the history of taxonomic classification, supported by citations.

claim: The data reveal that the Loxodonta lineage (as Palaeoloxodon) also colonized the Eurasian continent.
source: However, our data reveal that the Loxodonta lineage (as Paleoloxodon) also colonized the Eurasian continent.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phylogenetic results.

claim: The finding that L. africana is genetically more distant from L. cyclotis than is P. antiquus strongly supports previous evidence that urged recognition of L. cyclotis and L. africana as distinct species.
source: Last, the finding that L. africana is genetically more distant from L. cyclotis than is P. antiquus strongly supports previous evidence that urged recognition of L. cyclotis and L. africana as distinct species and underlines the importance of conservation efforts directed toward African forest elephants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phylogenetic results.

claim: The finding that L. africana is genetically more distant from L. cyclotis than is P. antiquus underlines the importance of conservation efforts directed toward African forest elephants.
source: Last, the finding that L. africana is genetically more distant from L. cyclotis than is P. antiquus strongly supports previous evidence that urged recognition of L. cyclotis and L. africana as distinct species and underlines the importance of conservation efforts directed toward African forest elephants.
evidence: This is a conclusion about conservation implications drawn from the phylogenetic results.

claim: In January 2014, a fragment of an elephant long bone was discovered during work at the Ehringsdorf quarries.
source: In January 2014, a fragment of an elephant long bone was discovered during work at the Ehringsdorf quarries.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the discovery of the specimen.

claim: The specimen was removed from the lower travertine (~3m above the base and 2.5 m below the Pariser horizon).
source: The specimen was removed from the lower travertine (~3m above the base and 2.5 m below the Pariser horizon), which has been dated by micro probe U/Th-series dating of primary travertine (Mallick and Frank, 2002) and ESR dating of tooth enamel (Schüler, 2003) to ~233 ka.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the stratigraphic context of the specimen.

claim: The lower travertine at Weimar-Ehringsdorf has been dated by micro probe U/Th-series dating of primary travertine and ESR dating of tooth enamel to ~233 ka.
source: The specimen was removed from the lower travertine (~3m above the base and 2.5 m below the Pariser horizon), which has been dated by micro probe U/Th-series dating of primary travertine (Mallick and Frank, 2002) and ESR dating of tooth enamel (Schüler, 2003) to ~233 ka.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to dating studies.

claim: Ten extracts were prepared from the Weimar-Ehringsdorf specimen using between 36 and 53 mg of bone material (totaling 425 mg).
source: Ten extracts were prepared using between 36 and 53 mg of bone (totaling 425 mg) material following the method of Dabney et al. 2013 (Dabney et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: 30 libraries were prepared from the Weimar-Ehringsdorf extracts using single-stranded library preparation with input volumes of 4, 8 and 12 µl DNA extract.
source: From these extracts, 30 libraries were prepared using single-stranded library preparation (Gansauge and Meyer, 2013) with input volumes of 4, 8 and 12 µl DNA extract (of 25 µl extract volume), respectively.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The number of library molecules was determined by digital droplet PCR using Bio-Rad's QX200 system with EvaGreen chemistry.
source: The number of library molecules was determined by digital droplet PCR using Bio-Rad's (Hercules, CA) QX200 system with EvaGreen chemistry (QX200 ddPCR EvaGreen Supermix, Bio-Rad) and primers IS7 and IS8 (Meyer and Kircher, 2010) following the manufacturer's instructions (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Libraries were amplified using AccuPrime Pfx DNA polymerase and labeled with two sample-specific indices.
source: Libraries were then amplified using AccuPrime Pfx DNA polymerase (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA) (Dabney and Meyer, 2012) and labeled with two sample-specific indices (Kircher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Ancient DNA work on the Neumark-Nord specimens was carried out in the ancient DNA laboratory at the University of Potsdam.
source: Ancient DNA work on the Neumark-Nord specimens was carried out in the ancient DNA laboratory at the University of Potsdam.
evidence: This is a statement about where the work was performed.

claim: Initially, eight Neumark-Nord specimens were screened for the presence of elephant DNA.
source: Initially, eight specimens were screened for the presence of elephant DNA of which the two best preserved ones (individual 23, Landesmuseum Halle museum inventory number HK 2007:25.285,117; a molar fragment [NEU2A] and a fragmentary upper jaw [NEU8B]; inventory number HK 92:990) were selected for further analyses.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: The two best preserved Neumark-Nord specimens (a molar fragment and a fragmentary upper jaw) were selected for further analyses.
source: Initially, eight specimens were screened for the presence of elephant DNA of which the two best preserved ones (individual 23, Landesmuseum Halle museum inventory number HK 2007:25.285,117; a molar fragment [NEU2A] and a fragmentary upper jaw [NEU8B]; inventory number HK 92:990) were selected for further analyses.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: In 2013, the petrous bone of individual 30 was sampled and also used in the analysis.
source: In addition, in 2013, the petrous bone of individual 30 (NEPEC; inventory number HK 2007:25:280 = E15.1.96) was sampled and also used in the analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the sampling.

claim: Fourteen DNA extracts were prepared from individual 30, and six from each of the two other Neumark-Nord specimens, using approximately 50 mg of bone powder in each extraction.
source: Fourteen DNA extracts were prepared from individual 30, and six from each of the two other specimens, using approximately 50 mg of bone powder in each extraction.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: DNA extraction and library preparation for Neumark-Nord specimens included Archaeoglobus fulgidus uracil-DNA glycosylase in library preparation, which removes the majority of uracils that are typically present in ancient DNA fragments.
source: DNA extraction and library preparation were performed as described above but including Archaeoglobus fulgidus uracil-DNA glycosylase in library preparation (Gansauge and Meyer, 2013), which removes the majority of uracils that are typically present in ancient DNA fragments.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: 52-mer capture probes for the enrichment of mtDNA sequences from elephants were designed using published mtDNA genome sequences of African forest elephant, Asian elephant, African savanna elephant and the mastodon.
source: 52-mer capture probes for the enrichment of mtDNA sequences from elephants were designed using the published mtDNA genome sequences of African forest elephant (NC_020759), Asian elephant (NC_005129), African savanna elephant (NC_000934) and the mastodon (NC_009574), with one probe starting at each position in these genomes.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Probes containing simple repeats longer than 24 bp were removed.
source: Probes containing simple repeats longer than 24 bp (repetition of the same 1–8 bp sequence motif) were removed.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Single-stranded biotinylated DNA probes were generated and used for two successive rounds of hybridization capture following a bead-based protocol.
source: Single-stranded biotinylated DNA probes were generated as described elsewhere (Fu et al., 2013) and used for two successive rounds of hybridization capture following a bead-based protocol (Maricic et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure, supported by citations.

claim: Enriched libraries were pooled and sequenced on one lane of a HiSeq2500 in paired-end mode (Weimar-Ehringsdorf libraries) or on an Illumina NextSeq 500 (Neumark-Nord libraries).
source: Enriched libraries were pooled and sequenced on one lane of a HiSeq2500 (Illumina, San Diego, CA) in paired-end mode (2 × 76 cycles plus 2 × 7 cycles index reads; Weimar-Ehringsdorf libraries) or on an Illumina NextSeq 500 (2 × 76 cycles plus 1 × 8 cycles index read; Neumark-Nord libraries).
evidence: This is a description of the sequencing procedure.

claim: Mapping of Weimar-Ehringsdorf data to the L. cyclotis mtDNA genome was performed using BWA and allowing up to five C to T substitutions but not more than three of other types.
source: To minimize the loss of alignments due to the high frequencies of damaged-induced substitutions in the Weimar-Ehringsdorf data, mapping to the L. cyclotis mtDNA genome (JN673264) was performed as previously described for the Sima de los Huesos mtDNA assemblies (Dabney et al., 2013), using BWA and allowing up to five C to T substitutions but not more than three of other types.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: The sequences from Neumark-Nord were mapped with 'ancient' parameters.
source: The sequences from Neumark-Nord were mapped with 'ancient' parameters as described elsewhere (Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: PCR duplicates were removed with bam-rmdup by calling a consensus from sequences with identical alignment start and end coordinates.
source: PCR duplicates were removed with bam-rmdup (Stenzel, 2014 Biohazard, available from https://bitbucket.org/ustenzel/biohazard) by calling a consensus from sequences with identical alignment start and end coordinates.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: Sequences shorter than 30 bp were discarded.
source: Sequences shorter than 30 bp were discarded.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: Several regions in the Weimar-Ehringsdorf mitochondrial genome showed more than one sequence variant, which derived from present-day human or microbial contamination.
source: When visually inspecting the Weimar-Ehringsdorf sequence alignments, we identified several regions in the mitochondrial genome where more than one sequence variant was present. Based on BLAST searches on a subset of these sequences, we found that they derived from present-day human or microbial contamination.
evidence: This is a statement about contamination identified in the data.

claim: Sequences that showed a greater similarity to contaminant genomes than to the African forest elephant mtDNA were removed from the Weimar-Ehringsdorf data.
source: We thus aligned all sequences to the identified contaminant genomes (GenBank accession nos. NC_012920, AF365635 and CP008889) and removed sequences that showed a greater similarity to one of the contaminants than to the African forest elephant mtDNA.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: No removal of contaminant sequences was necessary for the Neumark-Nord samples.
source: No removal of contaminant sequences was necessary for the Neumark-Nord samples.
evidence: This is a statement about the quality of the Neumark-Nord data.

claim: All T occurring in the first and last three positions of the Weimar-Ehringsdorf sequences were substituted by N to minimize the impact of damage-derived C to T substitutions on consensus calling.
source: To minimize the impact of damage-derived C to T substitutions on consensus calling, all T occurring in the first and last three positions of the Weimar-Ehringsdorf sequences were substituted by N.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: A position-based tabular output was generated from the alignment files using the 'mpileup' function of SAMtools.
source: Next, a position-based tabular output was generated from the alignment files using the 'mpileup' function of SAMtools (Li et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: The consensus was called at positions with minimum sequence coverage of 3 if the sequences were in at least 67.0% agreement.
source: This file was used to call the consensus at positions with minimum sequence coverage of 3 if the sequences were in at least 67.0% agreement.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: At three positions in the mtDNA genome (positions 384, 8467, 8469) with low consensus support, the consensus base was determined manually.
source: At three positions in the mtDNA genome (positions 384, 8467, 8469) with low consensus support, we spotted obvious alignment errors in one or all specimens and determined the consensus base manually.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: Apart from a ~500 bp stretch of repetitive sequence in the D-loop, only four positions remain undetermined in the Weimar-Ehringsdorf sequence and even fewer (between none and three) in the Neumark-Nord sequences.
source: Apart from a ~500 bp stretch of repetitive sequence in the D-loop, which cannot be reconstructed with short DNA fragments, only four positions remain undetermined in the Weimar-Ehringsdorf sequence and even fewer (between none and three) in the Neumark-Nord sequences.
evidence: This is a statement about the completeness of the mitochondrial genome sequences.

claim: Mitochondrial phylogenies were estimated using the software BEAST v 1.8.2 and a data set including 31 complete mitochondrial genomes.
source: We estimated mitochondrial phylogenies using the software BEAST (Drummond et al., 2012) v 1.8.2 and a data set including 31 complete mitochondrial genomes (GenBank accession nos.; L. cyclotis: JN673264, JN673263, KJ557424, KJ557423, KY616976, KY616979, KY616978; L. africana: WA4020, KR0014, KR0138, NC000934, DQ316069, AB443879; E. maximus: NC005129, DQ316068; M. primigenius: DQ316067, NC007596, EU155210, EU153449, EU153455, EU153456, EU153458, EU153445, EU153446, EU153447, EU153448, EU153452, EU153453, EU153454, JF912200; M. columbi: JF912199).
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: For three L. cyclotis individuals and three L. africana individuals, full genome sequences were obtained using previously collected samples and a specific amplification and sequencing strategy.
source: For three of the L. cyclotis individuals (LO3505, LO3508 and DS1511) and three L. africana individuals (WA4020, KR0014, KR0138), only partial mitochondrial sequences were previously published. Full genome sequences were obtained using previously collected samples (Ishida et al., 2013) and the amplification and sequencing strategy detailed by Brandt et al. (2012), except that additional primers were used in sequencing (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a description of the data generation procedure.

claim: The complete mitochondrial genome sequences were partitioned prior to analysis into four partitions, representing concatenated genes, tRNAs, rRNAs, and the control region.
source: The complete mitochondrial genome sequences were partitioned prior to analysis into four partitions, representing concatenated genes (with ND6 reversed), tRNAs, rRNAs, and the control region, and analyses were performed with and without the control region fragment.
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: All BEAST analyses were performed assuming the flexible skygrid coalescent model and the uncorrelated lognormal relaxed molecular clock.
source: All BEAST analyses were performed assuming the flexible skygrid coalescent model (Gill et al., 2013) and the uncorrelated lognormal relaxed molecular clock (Drummond et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The molecular clock was calibrated using the ages of ancient tips and a lognormal prior with a mean of 7.6 million years and standard deviation of 500,000 years for the divergence of the Loxodonta and Elephas/Mammuthus lineages.
source: We calibrated the molecular clock using the ages of ancient tips and a lognormal prior with a mean of 7.6 million years and standard deviation of 500,000 years for the divergence of the Loxodonta and Elephas/Mammuthus lineages (Rohland et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic analysis, supported by a citation.

claim: Ages of the ancient samples were sampled from normal distributions derived from stratigraphic and previously estimated radiometric dates: Neumark-Nord: 142–92 ka; Ehringsdorf 250–216 ka.
source: Ages of the ancient samples were sampled from normal distributions derived from stratigraphic and previously estimated radiometric dates: Neumark-Nord: 142–92 ka (Schüler, 2010); Ehringsdorf 250–216 ka (Mallick and Frank, 2002).
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic analysis, supported by citations.

claim: Separate evolutionary rates and models of nucleotide substitution were estimated for each partition in the alignment.
source: Separate evolutionary rates and models of nucleotide substitution, as estimated using jModelTest (Posada, 2008), were estimated for each partition in the alignment.
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Two MCMC chains were run for 60 million iterations each, with trees and model parameters sampled every 6000 iterations.
source: We ran two MCMC chains for 60 million iterations each, with trees and model parameters sampled every 6000 iterations.
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Chain convergence and parameter sampling were examined by eye using Tracer v 1.6.
source: Chain convergence and parameter sampling were examined by eye using Tracer v 1.6 (Rambaut A, Suchard MA, Xie D & Drummond AJ (2014) Tracer v1.6, available from http://beast.bio.ed.ac.uk/Tracer).
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The first 10% of samples were discarded from each run after which the two runs were combined.
source: The first 10% of samples were discarded from each run after which the two runs were combined.
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Trees were summarized and maximum clade credibility (MCC) trees identified using TreeAnnotator v 1.8.2.
source: Trees were summarized and maximum clade credibility (MCC) trees identified using TreeAnnotator v 1.8.2, which is distributed as part of the BEAST package.
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: MCC trees were edited and annotated using FigTree v1.4.2.
source: MCC trees were edited and annotated using FigTree v1.4.2 (http://tree.bio.ed.ac.uk/software/figtree/).
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Libraries from the three Neumark-Nord samples and another sample were pooled in equimolar concentrations and shotgun-sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 500 at Harvard Medical School.
source: Libraries from the three Neumark-Nord samples and another sample (not included in this study) were pooled in equimolar concentrations and shotgun-sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 500 (2 × 76 bp cycles) at Harvard Medical School.
evidence: This is a description of the sequencing procedure.

claim: Following determination of endogenous content and complexity in each library, two of them (NEPEC from the petrous bone and NEU2A from the molar fragment) were chosen for additional sequencing.
source: Following determination of endogenous content and complexity in each library, two of them (NEPEC from the petrous bone and NEU2A from the molar fragment) were chosen for additional sequencing and were pooled together with another sample (not included in this study) for one NextSeq 500 run.
evidence: This is a description of the sequencing strategy.

claim: Sequences were assigned to their source library according to their index allowing for one mismatch.
source: Sequences were assigned to their source library according to their index allowing for one mismatch.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: Adapters were trimmed and paired-end sequences were merged with SeqPrep 1.1 using default parameters but with a modification in the source code to retain the best base quality scores in the merged region.
source: Adapters were trimmed and paired-end sequences were merged with SeqPrep 1.1 (https://github.com/jstjohn/SeqPrep) using default parameters but with a modification in the source code to retain the best base quality scores in the merged region.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: Merged sequences shorter than 30 bp were discarded.
source: Merged sequences shorter than 30 bp were discarded.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: Alignment to the African savanna elephant reference genome (loxAfr4) was performed with BWA's version 0.7.8 using 'ancient' parameters and SAMtools' v.0.1.19 'samse' command.
source: Alignment to the African savanna elephant reference genome (loxAfr4; downloaded from ftp://ftp.broadinstitute.org/distribution/assemblies/mammals/elephant/loxAfr4/) was performed with BWA's version 0.7.8 (Li and Durbin, 2009) using 'ancient' parameters and SAMtools' v.0.1.19 'samse' command (Li et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: A custom script was used to remove duplicates, which takes into account the alignment coordinates of both ends of the sorted sequences and their orientation.
source: A custom script was used to remove duplicates, which takes into account the alignment coordinates of both ends of the sorted sequences and their orientation.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: From the first sequencing run, 47% and 35% of the sequences from the libraries from the petrous bone and the molar fragment (NEPEC and NEU2A, respectively) aligned to the reference genome.
source: From the first sequencing run, 47% and 35% of the sequences from the libraries from the petrous bone and the molar fragment (NEPEC and NEU2A, respectively) aligned to the reference genome while only 0.5% of the sequences from the third library (NEU8B) aligned to the reference genome.
evidence: This is a statement of the sequencing results.

claim: Only 0.5% of the sequences from the third library (NEU8B) aligned to the reference genome.
source: From the first sequencing run, 47% and 35% of the sequences from the libraries from the petrous bone and the molar fragment (NEPEC and NEU2A, respectively) aligned to the reference genome while only 0.5% of the sequences from the third library (NEU8B) aligned to the reference genome.
evidence: This is a statement of the sequencing results.

claim: The high percentage of mapped sequences in the petrous sample is consistent with previous reports on the superior DNA preservation in this part of the skeleton.
source: The high percentage of mapped sequences in the petrous sample is consistent with previous reports on the superior DNA preservation in this part of the skeleton (Gamba et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the sequencing results, supported by a citation.

claim: Following the second sequencing run, the total endogenous content of the first two libraries was estimated to 39% and 28%, with an average sequence length of 39 bp and 38 bp, respectively.
source: Following the second sequencing run, the total endogenous content of the first two libraries was estimated to 39% and 28%, with an average sequence length of 39 bp and 38 bp, respectively (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statement of the sequencing results.

claim: The average depth of coverage was 0.65-fold for NEPEC and 0.14-fold for NEU2A.
source: The average depth of coverage was 0.65-fold for NEPEC and 0.14-fold for NEU2A.
evidence: This is a statement of the sequencing results.

claim: Both NEPEC and NEU2A showed low frequencies of C to T substitutions at the 5' and 3' end, which are characteristic for Afu UDG-treated single-stranded libraries, except for in CpG context.
source: Both of them showed low frequencies of C to T substitutions at the 5' and 3' end, which are characteristic for Afu UDG-treated single-stranded libraries (Gansauge and Meyer, 2013), except for in CpG context, where deamination of 5-methylcytosine leaves thymine and not uracil (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a statement of the sequencing results, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Sequencing data from an African forest elephant (SL0001) that was sequenced to high-coverage at the Broad Institute was processed.
source: We also processed sequencing data from an African forest elephant (SL0001) that was sequenced to high-coverage at the Broad Institute and re-processed sequencing data of an Asian elephant from (Lynch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the data used in the analysis.

claim: Sequencing data of an Asian elephant from Lynch et al., 2015 was re-processed.
source: We also processed sequencing data from an African forest elephant (SL0001) that was sequenced to high-coverage at the Broad Institute and re-processed sequencing data of an Asian elephant from (Lynch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the data used in the analysis.

claim: The high-coverage genome of a woolly mammoth (Wrangel) from Palkopoulou et al., 2015 was used.
source: Moreover, we used the high-coverage genome of a woolly mammoth (Wrangel) from (Palkopoulou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the data used in the analysis.

claim: Pseudo-haploid consensus sequences for all autosomes of the two P. antiquus samples were called (~770 and ~210 million sites, respectively).
source: To determine the phylogenetic relationships between the two P. antiquus specimens and other members of the Elephantidae family, we called pseudo-haploid consensus sequences for all autosomes of the two P. antiquus samples (~770 and~210 million sites, respectively).
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: Sites with base quality below 30 and reads with mapping quality below 30 were filtered out.
source: Sites with base quality below 30 and reads with mapping quality below 30 were filtered out.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: To exclude post-mortem damage-derived C to T substitutions, 2 bp were trimmed from the ends of all reads.
source: To exclude post-mortem damage-derived C to T substitutions, we trimmed 2 bp from the ends of all reads.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: Regions of the loxAfr4 genome for which at least 90% of all possible 35-mers do not find a match at another position allowing for up to one mismatch were included.
source: We included regions of the loxAfr4 genome for which at least 90% of all possible 35-mers do not find a match at another position allowing for up to one mismatch, similar to the mappability filter described in (Prüfer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: A majority-allele calling rule that required at least one read aligned at each position of the genome was used.
source: We used a majority-allele calling rule that required at least one read aligned at each position of the genome.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: Using the same approach, sequences were called for an Asian elephant (Uno), a woolly mammoth (Wrangel) and an African forest elephant (SL0001).
source: Using the same approach, we called sequences for an Asian elephant (Uno [Lynch et al., 2015]), a woolly mammoth (Wrangel [Palkopoulou et al., 2015]) and an African forest elephant (SL0001; Broad Institute).
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: The reference sequence loxAfr4 was used as an African savanna elephant.
source: We also used the reference sequence loxAfr4, as an African savanna elephant.
evidence: This is a description of the data used in the analysis.

claim: The number of differences per base-pair for pairwise comparisons of all sequences was estimated and a distance matrix was constructed, from which a Neighbor-joining (NJ) tree was built using PHYLIP version 3.696.
source: We estimated the number of differences per base-pair for pairwise comparisons of all sequences and constructed a distance matrix, from which we built a Neighbor-joining (NJ) tree using PHYLIP version 3.696 (Felsenstein, 2005).
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: To obtain support values for the nodes of the tree, a bootstrap analysis (100 replicates) was performed by splitting all autosomes in blocks of 5 Mb and randomly sampling blocks with replacement and building a majority-rule consensus tree.
source: To obtain support values for the nodes of the tree, we performed a bootstrap analysis (100 replicates) by splitting all autosomes in blocks of 5 Mb and randomly sampling blocks with replacement and built a majority-rule consensus tree.
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Coding DNA sites (CDS) of protein-coding genes were extracted using the Ensembl 87 release for the loxAfr3 genome from each elephant genome sequence.
